item.title: Can GLP-1s Cure Addiction?
item.description:
Addiction

Can GLP-1s Cure Addiction?

Science suggests that GLP-1s may help conquer addiction, but history says no.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • GLP-1s, the hugely successful weight-loss drugs, show great promise for treating addiction.
  • History suggests their promise is overrated.
  • Large gaps between efficacy in the lab and effectiveness in the real-world must be addressed.
  • Psychological effects that maintain addiction cannot be ignored.

We’ve all likely heard of GLP-1s, the miracle Type 2 diabetes and weight loss drugs that slow digestion, control blood sugar, and signal satiation to the brain. The health effects of GLP-1-associated weight loss, as one might expect, are far-reaching and include reduced heart attack and stroke risk, better kidney and liver function, and improved sleep quality.

As it turns out, GLP-1s are also effective in curbing alcohol use and treating addiction. In the last two years, several scientific studies have shown GLP-1s to reduce cravings, decrease substance intake, and modulate addiction-related receptors in the brain.

These studies suggest great promise for GLP-1s in curing addiction. The New York Times, in bringing the good news to the public, called Ozempic a possible “breakthrough drug to conquer addiction.”

Such enthusiasm is understandable. Despite billions of dollars of federal, state, local, and private foundation funding, America’s struggles with addiction have deepened with each passing decade since the 1960s. Perhaps we’ve finally found the answer.

What History Says About Medical Cures for Addiction

There’s no disputing the science. GLP-1s work in curbing cravings and substance use for many of the people who take them. Given these findings, why would anyone want to rain on the GLP-1 parade? The answer is simple: We’ve seen this play and its encores before.

The first well-known drug treatment for alcohol use disorder was Antabuse (disulfiram). Antabuse causes an allergic-type reaction to drinking by blocking alcohol metabolism in the liver, with a resulting buildup of acetaldehyde, a toxin, in the body. Those who take Antabuse before drinking experience severe nausea, vomiting, flushing, and heavy sweating. These symptoms make Antabuse extremely effective in reducing alcohol intake.

Like GLP-1s, Antabuse was initially used for a different purpose—treating parasitic stomach infections—before its anti-alcohol use properties were discovered. Also like GLP-1s, Antabuse reduces cravings and has its own weight loss properties (albeit through different mechanisms), with associated improvements in organ function.

So why isn’t Antabuse, a drug that nearly abolishes alcohol intake in controlled studies, used regularly to treat alcohol use disorder? One reason is long-term side effects, but that’s true of common drugs used to treat a variety of physical ailments and mental health conditions.

More importantly, Antabuse only works for those who take it. Those who plan ahead of time to drink can stop taking Antabuse a few days beforehand. People like me, who work in the field, see this over and over again with Antabuse and other drug treatments for addiction. On the streets, where it counts most, drug treatments aren’t nearly as effective as they are in the lab. Suboxone, which I've written about elsewhere, provides another example.

Laboratory Versus Real-World Effectiveness

Source: Source data: Maisel et al. (2013); copyright T. Beauchaine

Two other drugs, naltrexone and acamprosate, were introduced in 1994 and 2004, respectively, to reduce cravings and treat addiction. Lab studies showed sizable reductions in alcohol cravings and alcohol use for both. A few years later, however, an analysis of 64 studies, including 10,933 people, found the effects of both drugs to be between negligible and small, as shown in the adjacent figure.

Other, non-pharmaceutical interventions have been framed as cures by our nation’s most senior public health officials: transcranial magnetic stimulation, deep brain stimulation, and low-intensity focused ultrasound. Effects in the lab are impressive, but on the streets the jury is still out. Why do we so often jump the gun in promising cures before testing our treatments in the real world?

What Lab Efficacy Doesn’t Capture

The difference between efficacy in the lab and effectiveness on the streets has been known to psychologists for decades. Why don’t highly effective treatments translate into real-world cures? In attempting to bridge the efficacy-to-effectiveness gap, medicine even invented a new field—implementation science. Progress, however, is limited.

Weak translation of efficacy into effectiveness isn’t restricted to addiction. Medical science has highly potent treatments for hypertension and heart disease, for example, but these aren’t adhered to by most patients either. Even vaccines that are 100 percent effective in preventing life-threatening viruses are rejected by ever-larger swaths of the population.

GLP-1s present a special challenge because their side effects, including nausea, vomiting, diarrhea, constipation, and stomachaches, can be intolerable. Although such effects can usually be managed with dietary restrictions, many people won’t accept such restrictions, and only a third of people treated with GLP-1s for pre-diabetic weight loss are adherent at one year. How can we expect GLP-1 treatments for addiction to be any different?

Between the laboratory and the real-world lies the human being. Psychology, more than any other discipline, should recognize this. Blocking the physiological effects of substances and managing cravings are important, but no magnetic field, ultrasound, or pharmaceutical can bring deserted children back, reverse financial ruin, heal the wreckage of infidelity, or resurrect someone killed by one’s drunk driving.

Events like these, which are common in addiction, diminish self-worth and engender legitimate shame—well-documented and potent catalysts for sustained use and relapse. Working through these emotions takes time. Short of erasing human memory and blunting human emotion, medical interventions will likely never be enough to cure addiction alone.

Too often we psychologists cede our expertise where it’s needed the most. Addiction treatment is one of those places. Take it from someone who knows.

item.title: 3 Ways Jealousy Can Threaten Your Relationship
item.description:
Jealousy

3 Ways Jealousy Can Threaten Your Relationship

Avoid these feelings of jealousy that can jeopardize your relationship.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Jealousy is a common experience in close relationships, an experience that can prove harmful.
  • New research identifies three goals in relationships and shows how perceptions of jealousy affect each one.
  • The more you prevent threat perception from outweighing relationship growth, the more you'll thrive.

Most people expect that once established, a long-term romantic relationship should be exclusive. All other potentially romantic connections should be severed, and the couple should be able to move on with their joint life, free of worry and strain.

Nevertheless, there are times when doubt comes into even the best relationship. Ellen and Oscar decided to move in together two years ago and, although marriage is in the works, they are waiting until their finances are in shape. Like any other couple, they go about their daily routines while they save for the future. Recognizing that they are still formally “single,” both of them avoid giving in to temptation if an attractive alternative comes along.

All of this was great until Ellen suspected that one of Oscar’s coworkers was trying to get, in her mind, uncomfortably close to him. The more she thought about this, the more she closed herself off emotionally to Oscar. She began to wonder if she should bother saving money for a future that might not happen while also resenting the time and effort she put into the exigencies of daily life such as meal planning and housework. Oscar swears he has no intention of straying, but her doubt only continues to grow.

A Three-Way Look at Relationship Dynamics

As defined in new research by University of Cologne’s Yael Ecker and colleagues (2026), jealousy is “a mental experience” composed of the negative emotions of sadness, anxiety, and anger as well as cognitive components such as “suspicious thoughts and lack of perceived control.” The bottom line is that jealousy, as a perception of threat, motivates people to try to protect their relationship. Unfortunately, this protection goal can crowd out the goal of keeping the relationship strong, consistent with the maintenance goal, in which couples focus on each other.

The U. Cologne authors propose that three types of goals characterize motivation in long-term relationships. We can use Ellen and Oscar as examples of each. Maintenance involves those behaviors Ellen engages in that keep things going on a daily basis. Progress is her motivation to save for the future. Protection refers to what Ellen is feeling as her jealousy begins to build.

Focusing primarily on the impact that jealousy has on relationship stability, Ecker et al. propose that when people distrust their partner’s loyalty, they, like Ellen, stop putting effort into those daily maintenance behaviors. Protection goals further impair relationship quality when partners think more about the threat (the coworker in this case) than their partner.

Testing Jealousy’s Impact on Relationship Stability

Across three studies varying in method, the authors tested the idea that, by lowering the healthy motivations of maintenance and progress, jealousy’s basis in protection creates a self-perpetuating cycle. In other words, the more jealous you are, the less you can focus on positive relationship goals.

article continues after advertisement

In the first study, an online sample of 400 U.K. residents was placed into two groups varying in prompts to think about a time when they felt jealous of their partner (jealousy induction) vs. an ordinary time in the relationship (control). Then they rated their relationship motivation according to maintenance, progress, and protection. The final piece of the study included questions about the individual’s relationship satisfaction, trust, and commitment. As it turned out, the jealousy induction indeed lowered levels of maintenance but also increased levels of progress motivation.

In the second study, the authors used a longitudinal design with 300 U.S. residents in long-term relationships to track feelings of jealousy across a two-week period along with their ratings of goal pursuit. As in the experimental study, jealousy increased protection strivings at the expense of maintenance. Also, as in the first study, jealousy led to increases in progress motivation.

Finally, the last study used an in-depth approach to study romantic pairs across a one-month period based on responses of 145 men and 142 women living in the U.K. (with relationship lengths of up to 46 years). As in the previous studies, jealousy predicted lower maintenance and higher progress striving. Perhaps some good news in this third study was that jealousy experiences tended to be rare and mild.

Putting Relationship Motivation to Work for You

Reviewing the three types of motivation, it appears that jealousy can indeed intrude on relationship satisfaction in the following three ways:

  1. Maintenance motivation: Jealous people spend more time focusing on an outside threat than on either behaving in ways that keep the couple going (i.e., daily tasks) or communicating positive feelings.
  2. Progress motivation: When people feel jealous, they may seek ways to change their relationship. But this is not always good. As the authors concluded, “constant improvement efforts may have detrimental effects or reflect underlying dissatisfaction.”
  3. Protection motivation: When people experience jealousy on a chronic basis, a self-perpetuating cycle exists that keeps protection high while diminishing maintenance.
article continues after advertisement

These findings suggest that people like Ellen would be better off focusing on their feelings for their partner than for looking for outside trouble. Furthermore, the stronger the protection striving, suggest the authors, the more you start to watch out for number one (i.e., yourself) rather than your partner. “Risk regulation theory,” they note, “posits that relationship threat triggers self-protection over connectedness goals.”

One tiny note in all of this relates to the difference between chronic and sporadic jealousy. Some small amount of jealousy once in a while could communicate to your partner strong feelings of love and commitment. Too much, though, will backfire.

To sum up, jealousy may be an inevitable part of all relationships, but it doesn’t have to spell a death sentence. By focusing on the factors that keep your relationship strong and moving in the right direction, the less likely it is that jealousy will rear its ugly head to spoil your fulfillment.

item.title: The Humanistic and Scientific Trajectories of Modern Psychiatry
item.description:
Psychiatry

The Humanistic and Scientific Trajectories of Modern Psychiatry

Psychiatry is at a crossroads as a caring and scientific profession.

Posted August 15, 2026

Key points
  • Psychiatry now follows an outdated scientific theory.
  • Psychiatry has a strong humanistic heritage.
  • A new guiding theory links humanism and science.

Modern psychiatry finds itself grappling with a dilemma. Its present guiding scientific philosophy or theory seems outdated to many in psychiatry, and they push for the modern systems approach now employed by all sciences except medicine. The impetus for this stems not only from a desire to become more scientific but also to reassert psychiatry’s traditional humanistic orientation.

Humanistic Psychiatry

Medicine itself has a strong humanistic tradition that dates to its origin with Hippocrates in the fifth century BC.1-3 But the advent of modern clinical medicine in the 18th century AD challenged this. Medicine began to view physical diseases as its primary focus, paying less heed to patients’ psychosocial and mental health issues. Reviewed previously, this stems from Descartes and the “mind-body split” theory.2-4

Martin Ferrell: Union City (2019)
Source: CC-BY-SA-3.0

Nevertheless, although accepting the idea that a brain disease caused mental symptoms, groups of general physicians rose to preserve the humanistic tradition.1 The care given to patients in what citizens called “insane asylums” or “lunatic asylums” appalled the doctors. This led them to coalesce over time to form the discipline of psychiatry in the 19th century. Their foremost goal was to provide “moral treatment” to asylum patients and rid the system of egregious practices such as poor control of filth and cessation of punitive practices (prolonged isolation, chain restraints, and corporal punishment, to name a few). Thus, the new psychiatry, alone in medicine, continued the ancient humanistic tradition.1,3,5

Psychiatry’s human orientation flourished and rose to its pinnacle in the first half of the 20th century under the influence of Sigmund Freud and his followers.6 His ideas vastly expanded the human dimensions of psychiatry, its impact continuing yet today. With the monumental discovery of the unconscious and its explanatory influence for human behaviors, psychiatry ensured that patients’ psychological and social features were paramount in diagnosis and treatment. And Freud’s identification of spontaneous free associations as the key to understanding the meaning of patients’ symptoms and actions resonates yet today in the field of patient-centered or person-centered communication.

Unforeseen health problems from the two world wars in the last century further countered the isolated disease focus held by medicine. Droves of soldiers returned home with what we now understand as post-traumatic stress disorder (then called “traumatic war neurosis” or “shell shock”). Clinicians understood soldiers’ anxiety (from war trauma) but were puzzled about the causes of their disabling physical symptoms such as insomnia, pain, weight loss, and fatigue because they found no disease explanation. Psychiatry thus established that symptoms could exist without an underlying disease explanation.7

article continues after advertisement

Nevertheless, despite this auspicious beginning for psychiatry, its powerful humanistic legacy would be displaced, but not eradicated, in the last half of the 20th century by promising scientific findings supporting the old idea of an underlying brain disease as the cause of mental illness.

Scientific Psychiatry

Theory is important,8 and understanding it is key to improving psychiatry’s practices from clinical care to education to research.9 Yet, most clinicians don’t recognize a theory’s impact despite having practiced based on its precepts for years.

Psychiatry’s present theoretical guidance, called the biomedical model, posits that the physical body, especially the brain, and its diseases cause mental disorders and their symptoms. Although this disease interest dates to the origin of psychiatry in the 19th century, there was little to support it until research in the last century produced powerful new drugs that suggested a possible chemical disorder causing a mental disease.1 The discoveries of lithium (1948) and chlorpromazine (1952) launched this and dramatically improved treatment for manic depression and schizophrenia, respectively. Benzodiazepines soon followed, and a cornucopia of ever more potent medications, such as modern antidepressants and antipsychotics, followed over the ensuing decades to provide a basis for the modern drug approach and its many successes. In parallel, tremendous technological advances led to vastly improved understanding of the brain and its circuitry and to the genetics of mental disorders, further encouraging the idea that some biological disorders caused mental illnesses.

Ralf Roletschek: Science library of Upper Lusatia in Görlitz, Germany.
Source: CC-BY-3.0; Self-published work

But the focus on disease causation of mental disorders has not panned out. Psychiatry has found no disease explanations after decades of research.10,11

Many in psychiatry demanded a new systems approach to provide a better understanding of mental disorders.9 This gained considerable momentum when George Engel articulated the biopsychosocial (BPS) model in 1977. It integrates the psychological and social dimensions of patients on an equal basis with their physical (biological) elements.12 In such a systems approach, multiple influences determine a mental illness—chemical, genetic, social, environmental, and psychological factors all interacting. That is, many dimensions are necessary, but no one in isolation explains a psychiatric disorder.11

article continues after advertisement

While medications continue to be important, we integrate their use with the patient’s psychological and social (environmental) issues. Indeed, research demonstrates that attending to the whole person using patient-centered interactions improves not only health outcomes but also the impact of medications themselves.13

Has there been progress? Now almost 50 years after Engel introduced the BPS model, most medical schools and psychiatry residencies embrace it in their mission statements,9 particularly since the patient-centered method needed to implement the model for each patient has recently rendered the BPS model fully scientific.14

And much recent psychiatry research has moved in a systems direction. For example, Kenneth Kendler15 and others propose that, rather than a disease, the many brain abnormalities observed represent critical causal pathways, and that mental disorders derive from multiple, interacting biological, psychological, and social influences.

Another systems-oriented research direction, articulated by Randy Nesse, is evolutionary psychiatry.16 It views the brain, unlike other organs, as an information-processing organ, and this vantage point proposes that psychiatric symptoms are coping mechanisms for various threats and opportunities. Some evolutionary ideas see mental symptoms as overdeveloped fight-or-flight or conversation-withdrawal responses that lead to, respectively, anxiety and depression. Others posit that symptoms are normal responses when understood in light of the patient’s traumatic developmental history.17

Further reflecting dissatisfaction with psychiatry’s disease-based perspective is the NIMH-supported Research Domain Criteria (RDoC) and a report by Tristram Lett et al., both of which indicate the need to integrate multiple biological, psychological, and social factors to understand mental disorders.18,19

The Future of Psychiatry (and Medicine)

The pendulum has swung away from psychiatry’s traditional interest in the personhood of its patients to focus on disease causes of mental disorders. But decades of research refute the idea. In a new direction, the biopsychosocial model has gained considerable traction and not only provides modern scientific guidance but also is more humanistic. At the same time, psychiatry’s new systems-based research suggests better explanations for mental disorders.

article continues after advertisement

Is the pendulum swinging back? By its intrinsic humanistic orientation and its quest for scientific precision, we find psychiatry poised to further blend science and humanism. And there’s more potential in doing this—leading the rest of medicine to more humane, more scientific practices.

Adapted from Has Medicine Lost Its Mind? (Prometheus Books, 2025).
